text:
Corn is monoecious, meaning it carries separate male and female flowers on the same plant. The male flower is the tassel at the top of the plant, which produces and sheds pollen; the female flower is the ear, lower on the stalk, wrapped in husk leaves with silks (the female flower's stigmas) extending from the tip. Each individual silk strand is connected to a single potential kernel on the cob, so a kernel can only form if its silk receives a pollen grain.

Successful pollination depends on timing: the tassel typically sheds pollen over several days, and the silks need to emerge and be receptive during roughly that same window (this synchrony is sometimes described using stages VT/tasseling and R1/silking). Silk colour and appearance change over time -- silks are pale/light when freshly emerged and receptive, and progressively darken and dry once pollinated or once they age past their receptive window.

Because pollination determines how many kernels actually form, the period around tasseling and silking (roughly stage R1) is one of the most sensitive periods in the crop's life to drought, heat, or nutrient stress -- stress at this stage can cause poor kernel set (blank patches on the cob) even if the plant otherwise looks healthy.
